title: Checkpoint: Animal Behavior
objective: After this level you can explain how instinct, learning and groups shape animal behavior.
summary: The 1973 Nobel honored von Frisch (bee dances), Lorenz (imprinting) and Tinbergen, whose dummy bills showed exaggerated features make supernormal stimuli.

cards.headline: Animal Behavior finale: one prize, three scientists, three animals.
cards.body: In 1973, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to three people who studied animal behavior: Karl von Frisch, Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. You've met two of them already. Let's line them up, then see Tinbergen's trick with fake beaks.

items.label: Karl von Frisch
points: Decoded the round and waggle dances

cards.fact: A fake can beat the real thing.
cards.context: Lorenz found that many instinctive acts are set off only by specific key stimuli. Tinbergen tested which features of a gull's bill trigger a chick's begging pecks, using dummies and varying shape, colors and contrasts. Exaggerate the right features and you get a supernormal stimulus: a fake that draws a stronger response than the real parent. That's why Level 71's chick aims at the red spot: the spot is the key, not the whole parent. The chick isn't recognizing Mom. It's answering a few key signals.

mascot.line: A cardboard bill outscoring a real parent. Instinct is a fast shortcut, not a careful judge.

Tools, mirrors and play: minds tested with care

questions.prompt: Animal Behavior recap: what is a supernormal stimulus?

options.label: A natural signal that fails to trigger instinct
options.rationale: It triggers a stronger response, not a weaker one.

options.label: An exaggerated fake that triggers a stronger response
A learned signal that replaces an instinct
options.rationale: It works on instinct, not learning.

options.label: A signal only adults can detect

questions.explanation: Tinbergen exaggerated key features on dummies and got stronger responses than to the real thing.

questions.prompt: Animal Behavior recap: why can a dummy bill fool a gull chick?

options.label: The chick has learned to love dummies
options.rationale: It needs no learning; the peck is innate.

options.label: The chick can't see at all
options.rationale: It sees the key features well enough.

options.label: The dummy smells like a parent
options.rationale: The test varied shape, colors and contrasts.

options.label: The chick responds to a few key features

questions.explanation: An instinct is set off by key stimuli, so a dummy with the right features works, and exaggerated ones work even better.

questions.prompt: Animal Behavior recap: which pairing of 1973 Nobel laureate and discovery is right?

options.label: Von Frisch: imprinting
options.rationale: Von Frisch decoded the bee dance.

options.label: Lorenz: the waggle dance
options.rationale: Lorenz studied imprinting in young birds.

questions.explanation: Lorenz studied imprinting, von Frisch the bee dance, Tinbergen key stimuli with dummies.

questions.prompt: Animal Behavior recap, from Level 74: where did the idea of the "alpha wolf" mostly come from?

options.label: Wild packs on Ellesmere Island
options.rationale: Mech saw no fights for the top spot there.

options.label: Ancient legends about wolves
options.rationale: It came from scientific studies, of the wrong wolves.

questions.explanation: Captive packs of unrelated wolves formed pecking orders; wild packs are families.

questions.prompt: Animal Behavior recap, from Level 78: dogs fail the mirror test but react to their own changed scent. What does that suggest?

options.label: A test depends on the sense it uses
Mirrors confuse every animal
options.rationale: Great apes, dolphins and others pass.

options.label: Smell tests are always easier
options.rationale: The point is matching the test to the animal.

questions.explanation: The mirror test is a sight test; dogs live by smell, so a smell test asks them a fairer question.
